artiest/larry-mizell.text:
Larry Mizell, born in 1944, was, with his brother Alphonso Fonce Mizell, one of the most important producers of the 1970s. Larry studied engineering and Fonce music at Howard University, where they sang together in the vocal quartet the Vanlords. Later Larry worked as an electrical engineer and carried out tests for the lunar module of NASA's Apollo programme. He was also among the first to carry out research into liquid crystals, which are now used in screens.

Fonce was a member of The Corporation, the team at Motown that wrote the early hits of The Jackson 5, such as I Want You Back and ABC. When Motown moved to Los Angeles, the brothers worked with the trumpeter Donald Byrd, with whom they had studied in Washington. Their first album together was Black Byrd on Blue Note, the first of a series that defined jazz-funk and laid the foundation for acid jazz and neo-soul. With their company Sky High Productions they also made records with The Blackbyrds, Johnny Hammond Smith and Roger Glenn, among others. Later came Boogie Oogie Oogie by A Taste of Honey in 1978 and Love Ballad by L.T.D. in 1976.

The brothers often used the same studio musicians and a warm, layered production with plenty of percussion. In the 1980s they withdrew, but in the 2000s they returned. In 2007 Larry co-wrote and sang on Play with the Changes by 4hero. Their work was regarded as a building block of jazz-funk, acid jazz and neo-soul.
artiest/larry-mizell.listen: Listen to Black Byrd by Donald Byrd and notice the tight, funky rhythm section and how the jazz trumpet keeps floating above it.

artiest/larry-morey.text:
Larry Morey was an American lyricist and screenwriter, born in Los Angeles in 1905. He was born with an incompletely formed left arm, and grew up without a mother: his father, a travelling ventriloquist, left him in a boarding house when he was six. Morey studied at UCLA, worked for Warner Bros. and Paramount and wrote, among other things, The World Owes Me a Living, to music by Leigh Harline, sung by Shirley Temple. In 1933 he went to Disney.

There he wrote for animated shorts and, with the composer Frank Churchill, for Disney's first feature-length animated film, Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs. Of the roughly twenty-five songs they wrote, eight remained in the film, including Heigh-Ho, Some Day My Prince Will Come, Whistle While You Work and I'm Wishing. The film received an Oscar nomination for best score. Morey also wrote the title song of Ferdinand the Bull, which won an Oscar in 1938, and with Perce Pearce adapted the book Bambi into the film of 1942. For Love Is a Song he received an Oscar nomination. In 1949 came a nomination for Lavender Blue, sung by Burl Ives.

Morey himself could play the piano only with difficulty, but was very musical. His songs are simple, cheerful and easy to sing along to, and are among the best known in the history of animation. Walt Disney is said to have seen him as an exception: an artist who kept on producing new work.
artiest/larry-morey.listen: Listen to Heigh-Ho from Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs and notice how the lyrics follow the marching tempo of the dwarfs and how the repetition almost turns the song into a work song.

artiest/larry-mullen-jr.text:
Larry Mullen Jr. is the drummer and co-founder of the Irish rock band U2. He was born in Dublin in 1961. As a boy he had piano lessons and he began drumming at the age of nine. For a time he played in marching bands and concert bands, where he mostly played the snare drum. At his secondary school, Mount Temple, he put a note on the notice board in 1976: drummer seeks musicians. In the kitchen at his home, Paul Hewson, later Bono, David Evans, later The Edge, and Adam Clayton, among others, came together. According to Mullen it was his band for ten minutes, until Bono walked in. After the names Feedback and The Hype, the group was called U2 from 1978.

With U2 Mullen made fifteen studio albums. His style is recognisable and almost military, a legacy of his time in the marching band. This can be heard clearly in Sunday Bloody Sunday. He uses his drum kit in a way of his own: because the bass drum was not his strongest point, from Pride (In the Name of Love) (1984) onwards he used a floor tom for that low sound. Under the influence of producers such as Daniel Lanois and Brian Eno he began to play more simply and leave more space open. Later, with the producer Flood, he learned to play along with drum machines and samples.

Mullen stays tightly on the beat, if anything slightly ahead of it rather than behind. His simple, powerful patterns form the foundation on which The Edge's guitar and Bono's voice can float. Outside U2 he made a dance version of the theme from Mission: Impossible (1996) with Clayton.
artiest/larry-mullen-jr.listen: Listen to Sunday Bloody Sunday by U2 and notice the opening: Mullen plays a tight march rhythm on the snare drum, as if a marching band were approaching. Hear how that rhythm keeps the whole song under tension.

artiest/larry-russell.text:
Larry Russell was an American composer, arranger and conductor who worked mainly for the film industry. He was born in Indiana in 1913 and died in Los Angeles in 1954, at the age of forty. His first success was in 1941, the song Oh For Heaven's Sake, which Alvino Rey recorded for Bluebird Records. He was married to the film composer Inez James, and together they also wrote for films.

Russell's best-known song is Vaya Con Dios, which he wrote in the early 1950s with Inez James and Buddy Pepper. It was recorded more than five hundred times and remained a standard. He wrote music for films such as Because of You from 1953 and conducted the orchestration of film scores for, among others, Crazy House, This Is the Life and Jolson Sings Again.

His work for Charlie Chaplin's film Limelight from 1952 brought him a posthumous Oscar. The film was not shown in Los Angeles until twenty years later, and under the rules of the time it therefore became eligible for the Academy Awards in 1972. Russell shared that prize with Raymond Rasch. In this way a composer who died young, with one song that went around the world and one Oscar that outlived his death, became a name in the history of film music.
artiest/larry-russell.listen: Listen to Vaya Con Dios in one of its many recordings and notice the simple, calm melody and the feeling of farewell that the chorus evokes.

artiest/larry-shields.text:
Larry Shields was an early American Dixieland clarinettist, born in Uptown New Orleans in 1893, on the same street as the pioneer Buddy Bolden. His brothers also played professionally. He began on clarinet at the age of fourteen and played in the bands of Papa Jack Laine. In the summer of 1915 he moved to Chicago as one of the first New Orleans musicians to do so, first with Bert Kelly and Tom Brown, and in November 1916 he joined the Original Dixieland Jass Band.

That band made the first jazz records the following year and brought Shields's playing to the attention of the whole of America. In 1921 he left the group, played in New York, briefly with Paul Whiteman, and moved to Los Angeles, where he led his own band and played brief roles in Hollywood films. In the 1930s he returned to Chicago with the reformed ODJB. He died in Los Angeles in 1953.

Shields co-wrote classics of the band, such as Clarinet Marmalade with Henry Ragas, and At the Jazz Band Ball, Ostrich Walk and Fidgety Feet with Nick LaRocca. His recordings were a model for later clarinettists, including Benny Goodman, and Dink Johnson began playing clarinet after hearing him. In 2006 his 1917 recording of Darktown Strutters' Ball was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame. He lets us hear how jazz sounded when it was still a new sound.
artiest/larry-shields.listen: Listen to At the Jazz Band Ball by the Original Dixieland Jass Band and notice the clarinet, which plays in fast, winding lines above the trumpet and the trombone.

artiest/larry-tee.text:
Larry Tee, born in Seattle in 1959, is an American DJ, club promoter and producer who brought the electroclash scene together in New York. He grew up in Seattle and in Marietta, Georgia, and moved to Atlanta in the early 1980s, where he hung out with RuPaul, Michael Stipe and Lady Bunny. In 1986 he moved to New York with RuPaul and others. There he became a figure in the Club Kids scene with his party Love Machine, and played in clubs such as Palladium, Roxy and Twilo.

In 1992 he co-wrote RuPaul's hit Supermodel (You Better Work). In the early 2000s, at the party Berliniamsburg, he trademarked the word electroclash. The word later found its way into the Oxford Dictionary. In 2001 he organised the Electroclash Festival, featuring Scissor Sisters, Fischerspooner and Peaches, among others. He also came up with the girl group W.I.T. In 2007 he made the song Matthew with Andy Bell, a tribute to Matthew Shepard. In 2009 his album Club Badd appeared, with Perez Hilton, Princess Superstar and Jeffree Star, among others. He also wrote for and with Afrojack, Shontelle, Santigold and Steve Aoki, and in 2014 launched the clothing line TZUJI.

His music is electronic, playful and provocative, with a direct, festive energy. Tee helped get the careers of RuPaul, Scissor Sisters, Fischerspooner and Peaches under way and showed how important a club promoter can be to pop history.
artiest/larry-tee.listen: Listen to Supermodel (You Better Work) by RuPaul and notice the tight dance beat and the confident, almost spoken vocals.

artiest/larry-young.text:
Larry Young was an American jazz organist, born in Newark, New Jersey, in 1940 and later also known as Khalid Yasin. In the 1950s he played in R&B bands and gained jazz experience with Jimmy Forrest, Lou Donaldson and Kenny Dorham, among others. He made his first records as a leader from 1960 for Prestige: Testifying, Young Blues and Groove Street. These are soul jazz, strongly influenced by Jimmy Smith.

Around 1964 he signed with Blue Note and his music began to show the influence of John Coltrane. He now made his most lasting work. He often played in a trio with the guitarist Grant Green and the drummer Elvin Jones, and Into Somethin' with the saxophonist Sam Rivers became his Blue Note debut. Unity from 1965 is his best-known album, with Joe Henderson and the young Woody Shaw. Later records such as Contrasts, Of Love and Peace and Heaven on Earth also drew in the avant-garde of the 1960s. After that he was one of the first musicians in fusion, on Emergency! with Tony Williams Lifetime and on Miles Davis's Bitches Brew. He also recorded a jam with Jimi Hendrix, which appeared after Hendrix's death on Nine to the Universe.

Young treated the Hammond B-3 organ in a modal, experimental way and away from the bluesy style of his predecessors. He often played percussively and used guitar-like and synthesizer-like effects. In 1978 he died in hospital at the age of 37, the precise cause of death being unclear.
artiest/larry-young.listen: Listen to Unity and notice how the organ does not merely play chords, but with free, open lines challenges the horns of Joe Henderson and Woody Shaw.

artiest/lars-danielsson.text:
Lars Danielsson is a Swedish jazz bassist, cellist and composer, born in Smålandsstenar in 1958. He studied at the conservatoire in Gothenburg, initially classical cello, but switched to jazz after being impressed by a concert by Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen. He plays double bass, electric bass and cello. In 1985 he formed a quartet with the saxophonist Dave Liebman, the pianist Bobo Stenson and the drummer Jon Christensen. That quartet was sometimes billed under his name and made several albums.

Danielsson has worked with a long list of jazz musicians, including John Scofield, Jack DeJohnette, Mike Stern, Billy Hart, Charles Lloyd, Terri Lyne Carrington, Leszek Możdżer, Tigran Hamasyan, Bugge Wesseltoft and Gino Vannelli. Under his own name he released records such as New Hands, Fresh Enough, Continuation, Far North, Our Standards, Fast Company, Shortcuts and Libera Me. Guests such as John Abercrombie, Kenny Wheeler, Bill Evans and Niels Lan Doky play on his albums.

He has also been active as a producer, including for Cæcilie Norby and the Danish radio orchestra. His music has a North European clarity, with plenty of room for melody and for the singing tone of his instrument. In this way Danielsson belongs among the Scandinavian bassists who have shaped the sound of European jazz.
artiest/lars-danielsson.listen: Listen to a track from Libera Me and notice the bass or cello, which puts the melody in front and moves through the piece almost singing.

artiest/lars-ulrich.text:
Lars Ulrich is the drummer and co-founder of the American metal band Metallica. He was born in Gentofte, near Copenhagen, in 1963, the son of the tennis player Torben Ulrich. The jazz saxophonist Dexter Gordon was his godfather. At the age of nine he saw Deep Purple in Copenhagen, and the next day he bought their album Fireball. Around the age of thirteen he got his first drum kit. In 1980 he moved to California to become a tennis player, but chose music. He fell under the spell of the New Wave of British Heavy Metal, especially the band Diamond Head.

In 1981 he placed an advertisement in a local magazine. The guitarist and singer James Hetfield responded, and together they started Metallica. Ulrich and Hetfield wrote almost all the songs together and are the only members who have been there from the beginning. In the 1980s Ulrich became known for his fast, aggressive thrash beats, on albums such as Kill 'Em All, Ride the Lightning, Master of Puppets and ...And Justice for All. He used two bass drums and a hard china cymbal instead of the usual ride cymbal. From the album Metallica (1991) he began to play more simply, fitting the more hard-rock-oriented songs.

In 2000 Ulrich became the face of Metallica's lawsuit against Napster, the service through which music was shared for free. The band discovered that even a still unfinished song, I Disappear, was already circulating. Ulrich spoke in the US Senate, and the case was settled out of court. Many fans found it strange that a rich rock band should take on its own listeners. In this way a drummer found himself in the middle of the debate about music in the internet age.
artiest/lars-ulrich.listen: Listen to One by Metallica and notice the last section: Ulrich plays lightning-fast, even strokes on two bass drums, like a machine gun. Hear how that contrasts with the quiet, almost restrained beginning of the song.

artiest/lata-mangeshkar.text:
Lata Mangeshkar was born in 1929 in Indore, in present-day India, as Hemalata Mangeshkar. Her father Deenanath was a classical singer and stage actor. She became a playback singer, someone who sings the songs in films on behalf of the actors, and sometimes also a composer. Her career lasted eight decades. She recorded songs in more than thirty-six Indian languages and a few foreign ones, above all in Hindustani, Bengali and Marathi. She died in 2022.

She was known for her discipline. She always recorded her songs barefoot, out of respect for the recording studio, which she saw as a temple. Although she was a perfectionist, by her own account she never listened to her songs after they were released, because she would hear only mistakes. In 1974 she was the first Indian playback singer to perform at the Royal Albert Hall in London. She was listed in the Guinness Book of Records as the most recorded artist, until her sister Asha Bhosle replaced her.

In 1989 she received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award and in 2001 the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour, as the second woman singer to do so. In 2009 France appointed her an officer of the Legion of Honour. She was called the Queen of Melody. Her voice is high, clear and light, and her songs gave Indian film music a face with which the whole subcontinent could identify. Pyar Kiya To Darna Kya from 1960 and Aaj Phir Jeene Ki Tamanna Hai from 1965 are well-known examples.
artiest/lata-mangeshkar.listen: Listen to Aaj Phir Jeene Ki Tamanna Hai. Notice the clear, light voice and how she moves through a long melody without forcing.

artiest/laurent-garnier.text:
Laurent Garnier, also known as Choice, is a French producer and DJ, born in 1966. In 1984 he worked as a waiter at the French embassy in London. In 1986 he moved to Manchester, where he discovered the flourishing British house scene and began to play records. In 1987 he came to The Haçienda and played there under the name DJ Pedro, when Chicago house and Detroit techno were becoming popular. In New York he met Frankie Knuckles.

In the early 1990s he returned to France. For three years he organised the Wake Up parties at the Rex Club in Paris and played in Dijon, at Le Palace and at raves. For the label FNAC he made French Connection and the EP A Bout de Souffle. He then founded the label F Communications with Eric Morand. His first album was Shot in the Dark, followed by 30 in 1997, with the single Crispy Bacon. In 2000 came Unreasonable Behaviour, with The Man with the Red Face, one of his best-known tracks. Later albums are The Cloud Making Machine, Tales of a Kleptomaniac and Le roi bâtard.

His music is techno and house with a heavy, danceable rhythm, and he often plays long sets. Garnier is regarded as a pioneer of French techno and remains a fixture at the big festivals. He shows how a DJ, who at first only plays records, can also build a label and a sound of his own.
artiest/laurent-garnier.listen: Listen to The Man with the Red Face and notice how the track grows out of a small, repeated figure and how the electronic beat runs firmly beneath everything.

artiest/laurie-anderson.text:
Laurie Anderson is an American avant-garde artist, musician and filmmaker, born in Chicago in 1947. She had violin lessons, studied art history at Barnard College and in 1972 took a master's degree in sculpture at Columbia University. She performed her first performance piece, a symphony for car horns, in 1969. In the 1970s she worked in New York as an art teacher, art critic and performer, with an emphasis on language, technology and image. A well-known piece from that time is Duets on Ice, in which she played on skates that were frozen into a block of ice and stopped only when the ice had melted.

Her commercial breakthrough came unexpectedly in 1981, when O Superman reached number two in the British chart. In 1982 her debut album Big Science followed, then Mister Heartbreak, Strange Angels, Bright Red and Life on a String. In 1986 she starred in and directed the concert film Home of the Brave. She also made theatre work, documentaries, installations and a CD-ROM.

Anderson is a pioneer in electronic music and invented instruments of her own for her recordings and shows. Her music combines storytelling, violin sounds and electronics, with a cool, dry voice that almost speaks. She showed that pop and performance art can reinforce each other, and her work opened a path for artists who want to combine music, image and technology.
artiest/laurie-anderson.listen: Listen to O Superman and notice the repeated, electronic sound beneath her voice, and how the story about a telephone call sounds almost like a monologue.

artiest/lauryn-hill.text:
Lauryn Hill was born in 1975 in East Orange, New Jersey, into a family full of music. Her mother played piano, her father sang in nightclubs, and at home Curtis Mayfield, Stevie Wonder, Aretha Franklin and Marvin Gaye were played. At school she founded a gospel choir. As a teenager she appeared in a soap opera and in the film Sister Act 2 (1993). She became known as a singer and rapper with the Fugees, with Wyclef Jean and Pras Michel. Their album The Score (1996), with Killing Me Softly and Ready or Not, won a Grammy for best rap album. Hill was the first woman to win that prize.

Her solo album The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill appeared in 1998. It mixes hip hop with soul, reggae and doo-wop, and Hill alternates between rapping and singing as if they were one language. The first single, Doo Wop (That Thing), went straight to number 1 in the United States. Ex-Factor and Everything Is Everything also became hits. At the 1999 Grammy ceremony she won five awards in one evening, the first woman ever to do so, and the first rapper to win the prize for album of the year.

After that one studio album Hill largely withdrew. She still appeared on the live album MTV Unplugged No. 2.0 (2002) and wrote and produced for others, such as Aretha Franklin and Whitney Houston. Even so she is regarded as one of the most important figures of neo-soul and as a pioneer of melodic rapping, who showed that rap and singing need not be separate.
artiest/lauryn-hill.listen: Listen to Doo Wop (That Thing) and notice how Lauryn Hill raps in the verses and sings in the chorus. Also hear the horns and the backing vocals, which hark back to the soul and doo-wop of the 1960s.

artiest/laverne-andrews.text:
LaVerne Andrews was born in Minneapolis in 1911 and was the eldest of the Andrews Sisters, an American close-harmony group from the swing and boogie-woogie era. She sang alto, her sister Maxene soprano and her sister Patty mezzo-soprano. Their father was Greek, their mother Norwegian. LaVerne played piano for silent films in exchange for dance lessons for the girls. When the sisters won a talent contest in Minneapolis, Patty was twelve. After their father's restaurant went bankrupt, they went on tour to support the family.

The sisters began as imitators of the Boswell Sisters, and came to national attention in 1937 with Bei Mir Bist Du Schön, a big hit for Decca. Beer Barrel Polka followed in 1939, Beat Me Daddy, Eight to the Bar in 1940, Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy in 1941, Don't Sit Under the Apple Tree in 1942 and Rum and Coca-Cola in 1945, which introduced American listeners to calypso. They are estimated to have sold eighty million records.

The tight three voices over a swinging rhythm became their trademark. Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy is regarded as an early example of jump blues. Later singers such as Patti Page, Bette Midler, the Pointer Sisters and Pentatonix took over their harmonies. LaVerne died in 1967. In 1998 the group was among the first inductees of the Vocal Group Hall of Fame.
artiest/laverne-andrews.listen: Listen to Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy and notice how the three voices glide through the song almost like a single instrument, locked tightly to the boogie-woogie rhythm.

artiest/lawrence-tibbett.text:
Lawrence Tibbett was an American opera singer, born in Bakersfield, California, in 1896. His father, a deputy sheriff, was shot dead in 1903. Tibbett grew up in Los Angeles and earned money by singing in church choirs and at funerals. After the First World War he sang in a cinema showing silent films, and he studied in New York with Frank La Forge. In 1923 he signed his first contract with the Metropolitan Opera. Through a mistake his name acquired an extra t, and he kept that spelling.

From 1923 to 1950 he sang leading roles at the Met more than six hundred times. He sang, among others, Valentin in Faust, Tonio in Pagliacci and the Herald in Lohengrin. His national breakthrough came with the role of Ford in Verdi's Falstaff. He toured Europe and Australia and also did musical theatre and radio. His first film, The Rogue Song from 1930, earned an Oscar nomination for best actor. From 1926 he made his recordings exclusively for Victor, later RCA Victor, including excerpts from Porgy and Bess.

Tibbett was a baritone with a large, deep, dark voice, which could range from powerful forte to delicate pianissimo. He combined a beautiful voice with great musicality and a strong stage presence. As an American who built a complete career in his own country, he was one of the first great American opera stars who also reached the wider public through film and radio.
artiest/lawrence-tibbett.listen: Listen to his recording of excerpts from Porgy and Bess and notice the dark, full tone of his voice and how he can also make it sound soft.

artiest/le-concert-d-astree.text:
Le Concert d'Astrée is a French ensemble for instrumental and vocal Baroque music. The conductor and harpsichordist Emmanuelle Haïm founded it in 2000. Since 2004 the ensemble has been affiliated with the Opéra de Lille and has built an international reputation with the repertoire of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. In 2003 it was named best ensemble of the year at the Victoires de la musique classique, and in 2008 it won the Echo Deutscher Musikpreis in the category Alte Musik.

The records show its breadth. There are opera recordings, such as Purcell's Dido and Aeneas and Monteverdi's L'Orfeo, and Handel's Il trionfo del Tempo e del Disinganno. In addition Delirio, Combattimento, a Mass in C and a combination of Bach's Magnificat with Handel's Dixit Dominus have appeared. There is also Carestini: The Story of a Castrato, a record about a famous eighteenth-century castrato.

The ensemble plays Baroque music with a lively, dramatic accent, as befits opera. In this way it brings the work of Purcell, Monteverdi, Bach and Handel closer to a modern audience, and it belongs among the French groups that gave authentic performance practice a face of its own.
artiest/le-concert-d-astree.listen: Listen to an aria from Dido and Aeneas and notice the slowly descending bass line beneath the voice, and how the voice above it almost becomes a lament.

artiest/le-concert-des-nations.text:
Le Concert des Nations is an orchestra that plays the orchestral and symphonic repertoire from the Baroque to the Romantic period, roughly from 1600 to 1900, on historical instruments. The Catalan conductor and viola da gamba virtuoso Jordi Savall founded it in 1989. It is the youngest of his groups and the first orchestra of its kind to consist largely of musicians from Latin countries, including Spain, South America, Italy, Portugal and France. It is also the orchestra of La Capella Reial de Catalunya.

The name refers to the work of François Couperin, in which different national tastes come together, and bears the traces of the Enlightenment. In 1992 the orchestra made its opera debut with Una Cosa Rara by Vicente Martín y Soler, at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, the Gran Teatre del Liceu and the Auditorio Nacional. The records include Bach's Les Quatre Ouvertures, the Brandenburg Concertos, Handel's Water Music and Music for the Royal Fireworks, Mozart's Requiem and Haydn's Les sept dernières paroles de notre Rédempteur sur la Croix.

By playing on instruments of the period, with a colourful, light and lively sound, the orchestra lets us hear how Baroque and Classical music may originally have sounded. It also brings back rarely played works and has thus contributed to the rise of historically informed performance.
artiest/le-concert-des-nations.listen: Listen to Handel's Water Music and notice the sound of the historical instruments, which is lighter and sharper than that of a modern symphony orchestra.

artiest/le-grand-kalle.text:
Joseph Athanase Tshamala Kabasele, better known as Le Grand Kallé, was a Congolese singer, composer, record boss and founder of African Jazz. He was born in 1930 in Pala Bala, near Matadi, into a Luba family, and moved a week later to Léopoldville, present-day Kinshasa. He received more education than many of his contemporaries and worked for a time as a typist. After working with a group of session musicians, he founded African Jazz in 1953, the first fully modern Congolese band to record in the studio.

He brought traditional Congolese instruments, such as the Tetela tam-tam, the ngongi and the lokole, together with a worldly rumba with layered guitar playing and melodic vocal phrases. Guitarists such as Tino Baroza, Dechaud Mwamba and Nico Kasanda laid the foundations of the Congolese rumba guitar, which for years rang out across East, Central and West Africa. In 1960 Kabasele and African Jazz played the song Indépendance Cha Cha at the Belgian-Congolese Round Table Conference in Brussels, which became a symbol of decolonisation and unity. That same year he became the first Congolese musician to start a label of his own, Surboum African Jazz.

After internal ruptures in the band he founded African Team in Paris in 1969, and in 1970 the album L'African-Team appeared. In his later years he somewhat faded into the background, but remained respected, and in 1980 the musicians' union named him grand maître of Zairean music. He died in Paris in 1983. Kabasele is regarded as the father of modern Congolese popular music.
artiest/le-grand-kalle.listen: Listen to Indépendance Cha Cha and notice the light guitar lines, the light dance tempo and the shared chorus, which brings celebration and politics together in a single song.

artiest/le-grand-kalle-en-l-african-jazz.text:
Le Grand Kallé et l'African Jazz was one of the most influential Congolese rumba bands of the twentieth century. Joseph Kabasele, better known as Le Grand Kallé, founded the group in 1953 in Léopoldville, present-day Kinshasa. The band did not play jazz. In Belgian Congo the word jazz stood for elegance and liveliness, and that stuck to the name. The group combined traditional Congolese instruments, such as drums, with Western instruments and was known for its Congolese rumba.

The first successes came in November 1953 with recordings such as Parafifi, Nzela mosika and African Jazz. The guitarist Nico Kasanda played an important part in these. In the 1950s the group faced competition from OK Jazz, the band of Franco Luambo among others. In January 1960 African Jazz travelled to Brussels, where the Belgian-Congolese Round Table Conference on independence took place. It was the first Congolese band to perform there. Indépendance Cha Cha dates from that same year.

From 1963 important members left the group, including Tabu Ley Rochereau and Nico Kasanda, who founded African Fiesta. In this way the original line-up fell apart. Even so, African Jazz determined how modern Congolese pop music sounded in the late colonial years and the first years after independence.
artiest/le-grand-kalle-en-l-african-jazz.listen: Listen to Indépendance Cha Cha and notice the cha-cha-cha rhythm with the soft, singing guitars. Do you hear how the voice and the choral singing alternate?

artiest/le-mystere-des-voix-bulgares.text:
Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares is the name under which the women's choir of the Bulgarian state broadcaster became known. The choir was founded in 1952 by Georgi Boyadjiev and performs modern arrangements of Bulgarian folk melodies. The singers are chosen from villages, for the beauty and openness of their voices, and undergo a long training in the age-old singing style. The choir received its name from the Swiss ethnomusicologist Marcel Cellier, who spent fifteen years working to get the recordings released.

The first album appeared in 1975. The choir became internationally known when the British label 4AD reissued two compilation albums in 1986 and 1988. The second volume won a Grammy in 1989. The music is influenced by Thracian, Bulgarian, Ottoman and Byzantine history. It uses diaphonic singing, a distinctive vocal timbre, modal scales, unusual time signatures and clashing harmonies with many seconds, sevenths and ninths.

In the 1990s the choir became known in the United States through the music of the series Xena: Warrior Princess, whose theme is derived from Kaval sviri. Three soloists of the choir also sang as Trio Bulgarka on albums by Kate Bush. In this way the choir brought Bulgarian folk music to a Western pop audience.
artiest/le-mystere-des-voix-bulgares.listen: Listen to Kaval sviri and notice the tense, grating harmonies between the voices. Try to hear where the high voices and the low drone sound together.

artiest/lead-belly.text:
Lead Belly's real name was Huddie Ledbetter. He was born around 1889 on a plantation near Mooringsport, Louisiana, and grew up in Texas. His uncle gave him an accordion, but he became known above all as a singer with a twelve-string guitar. As a teenager he was already playing in the bars and dance halls of Shreveport. His life was rough: he was in prison several times, including for manslaughter. In 1933 the folklorists John Lomax and his son Alan discovered him in Angola prison in Louisiana, where they were recording folk music for the Library of Congress.

After his release in 1934 he travelled with John Lomax and in 1935 came to New York. The newspapers wrote about the convict who had sung his way to freedom, a story that was not true but sold well. His first commercial records sold poorly. He eventually found his audience among folk enthusiasts: he played with Woody Guthrie, Pete Seeger, Sonny Terry and Brownie McGhee. In 1940 he recorded The Midnight Special and Other Southern Prison Songs for RCA Victor, and in the 1940s he made records for Moses Asch, the later founder of Folkways. He died in 1949.

Lead Belly sang gospel, blues, work songs, children's songs and ballads about imprisonment, cotton picking and racism. Many of those songs became standards: Goodnight, Irene, Midnight Special, Cotton Fields, Black Betty, Rock Island Line and In the Pines, also known as Where Did You Sleep Last Night. Through the folk revival they reached later generations of rock and pop musicians. In this way he became a link between the old Black folk music of the South and the pop music that came later.
artiest/lead-belly.listen: Listen to Where Did You Sleep Last Night by Lead Belly and notice the twelve-string guitar, which sounds fuller and rougher than an ordinary guitar. Hear how his voice shoots up at the end of the lines and hangs there. Then put Nirvana's 1993 version next to it.

artiest/lebo-m.text:
Lebohang Morake, known as Lebo M, is a South African producer and composer. He was born in Soweto in 1964, received no musical training and left school at the age of nine to sing in nightclubs. He recorded his first single, Celebration, at thirteen, for twenty dollars. At fifteen he worked in Maseru in Lesotho, where he lived in exile because of apartheid. The ambassador of Lesotho to the United States helped him to an art academy in America. At eighteen he moved to Los Angeles, did all sorts of odd jobs and studied at Los Angeles City College.

The breakthrough came through Johnny Clegg's producer, Hilton Rosenthal, who put him in touch with the composer Hans Zimmer. Together they wrote the music for The Power of One. Morake also used his knowledge of African rhythms for films such as Congo and Outbreak. Zimmer recommended him to Disney for The Lion King. He formed and conducted the African choir that sings in the film, and co-wrote and sang on the soundtrack and in the stage version. Later came records such as Rhythm of the Pride Lands from 1995 and the music for Mufasa: The Lion King from 2024.

His music brings South African choral singing and rhythms into Hollywood film music. The opening cry of The Lion King, sung in Zulu, made an African voice a globally recognisable sound in popular culture.
artiest/lebo-m.listen: Listen to the opening of The Lion King, the song Circle of Life, and notice the Zulu singing at the start and how the choir then carries the whole song.

artiest/ledisi.text:
Ledisi Anibade Young, Ledisi for short, is an American singer, songwriter, producer, author and actress, born in New Orleans in 1972. Her name means in Yoruba that something is brought forth. Her mother sang in a local band, and her biological grandfather was the bluesman Johnny Ace of Pledging My Love. At the age of eight she performed with the New Orleans Symphony Orchestra. When she was thirteen the family moved to Oakland, California.

In 1995 she formed a band and, with Sundra Manning, started the label LeSun Music when a major label did not sign her. Her first album, Soulsinger, contained the single Take Time, which received a great deal of airplay on radio in the San Francisco region. Feeling Orange but Sometimes Blue from 2002 won a jazz award at the California Music Awards. In 2006 she signed with Verve Forecast, and Lost & Found earned her two Grammy nominations, including one for best new artist. It's Christmas, Turn Me Loose, Pieces of Me, The Truth and Let Love Rule followed. On her own label she released The Wild Card, with Anything for You, which won a Grammy, and later Ledisi Sings Nina.

Ledisi sings soul, jazz, gospel and R&B with a powerful voice and a great deal of freedom in her phrasing. She played Mahalia Jackson in the film Selma and later Gladys Knight in Spinning Gold. In this way she became a well-known voice in contemporary soul.
artiest/ledisi.listen: Listen to Anything for You and notice how she builds calmly with a warm, full voice and lingers just a little longer on certain words.

artiest/ledward-ka-apana.text:
Ledward Kaapana was born in 1948 and grew up in Kalapana, a small village on a black sand bay on Hawaii, which was largely destroyed in 1986 by an eruption of Kilauea. There was no electricity, no television and hardly any radio, so the family made its own music. His mother Tina and his uncle Fred Punahoa, a rarely recorded master of slack key, taught him to play. Slack key is a Hawaiian guitar style in which the strings are tuned to open tunings.

As a teenager he founded the group Hui Ohana with his twin brother Nedward and his cousin Dennis Pavao, which released fourteen albums. Later he led the trio I Kona. His first solo album, Lima Wela from 1983, won a Na Hoku Hanohano Award in 1984. Led Live in 1994 and Black Sand in 2000 were among those that followed. He also recorded with the lap steel player Bob Brozman.

Kaapana plays with thumb and forefinger and uses fingerpicks. He combines old phrases with modern influences and improvisation into polyphonic arrangements. He sings as a baritone and in falsetto. The country guitarist Chet Atkins was so impressed that he gave him his guitar. In 2011 Kaapana received a National Heritage Fellowship, the highest American honour for folk art. In this way he preserves a Hawaiian tradition and keeps it alive.
artiest/ledward-ka-apana.listen: Listen to Radio Hula and notice how the guitar plays a melody, a bass line and a rhythm at the same time. Try to hear whether the voice is singing in falsetto.

artiest/lee-konitz.text:
Lee Konitz was an American alto saxophonist and composer. He was born in Chicago in 1927, the son of Jewish immigrants. At eleven he was given a clarinet, inspired by Benny Goodman, but out of admiration for Lester Young he switched to the tenor saxophone and later to the alto. In 1945 he began as a professional musician. A year later he met the pianist Lennie Tristano, who would influence him strongly. In 1947 he played in Claude Thornhill's orchestra, where Gil Evans arranged and Gerry Mulligan composed.

In 1948 he became a member of Miles Davis's nonet. The recordings of that group from 1949 and 1950 later appeared as Birth of the Cool, one of the sources of Cool Jazz. Davis was criticised for hiring a white saxophonist, but replied that he would hire anyone who played as well as Konitz. In 1949 he also recorded early free improvisations with Tristano and the saxophonist Warne Marsh. His first albums as a leader were later collected on Subconscious-Lee. He then played in Stan Kenton's orchestra and with Gerry Mulligan. His trio album Motion (1961) is regarded as a high point. He kept on playing into old age, including free jazz and avant-garde. He died in 2020 of the effects of COVID-19.

At a time when almost every alto saxophonist imitated Charlie Parker, Konitz found a sound of his own: light, dry and without much vibrato. He played long, melodic lines with unexpected accents. In this way he influenced saxophonists such as Paul Desmond and Art Pepper.
artiest/lee-konitz.listen: Listen to Subconscious-Lee and notice Konitz's tone: light and clear, almost without vibrato. Hear how he plays long, winding lines in which the accents keep falling in unexpected places.

artiest/lee-morgan.text: The trumpeter Lee Morgan, from Philadelphia, was taught as a teenager by Clifford Brown, his great role model. At eighteen he played in Dizzy Gillespie's big band and made his first records for Blue Note. He also played on John Coltrane's Blue Train. From 1958 to 1961 he was the trumpeter of Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers. His playing was fiery, playful and full of blues phrases. In 1963 he recorded The Sidewinder, whose title track became a kind of jazz dance number; the album was one of Blue Note's best-selling records. In February 1972 he was shot dead between two sets in a New York club by his partner Helen Morgan.
artiest/lee-morgan.listen: Hear the short, bluesy trumpet phrases above a danceable rhythm.

artiest/lee-scratch-perry.text:
Lee 'Scratch' Perry's real name was Rainford Hugh Perry. He was born in 1936 in Kendal, in rural Jamaica. After the age of fifteen he worked as a labourer, until he moved to Kingston. At the end of the 1950s he began as a record seller for Coxsone Dodd's sound system and did all sorts of jobs in his studio, Studio One. After quarrels over money he left for Joe Gibbs, and in 1968 he started his own label, Upsetter Records. His single People Funny Boy, a jibe at Gibbs, used the sound of a crying baby and had a fast, chopping rhythm that would soon be called reggae.

With his studio band The Upsetters he scored a hit in England in 1969 with the instrumental The Return of Django. Around 1970 he worked with Bob Marley and The Wailers, and he encouraged the engineer to use reverb and echo. In 1973 he built a studio of his own in his back garden, the Black Ark. There he worked for days on his mixes, with only four tracks, which he kept bouncing down to make room for new layers. He recorded Junior Murvin, Max Romeo and The Congos there, among others. Super Ape (1976) is regarded as the high point of that period. Around 1978 the studio fell into decline and burned down; Perry himself said that he had set the fire.

Perry was, together with King Tubby, one of the pioneers of dub. He made new versions of existing songs with echo, reverb and loose sound fragments, and was already thinking of the later mixes while recording. Later he worked with The Clash, Adrian Sherwood and the Beastie Boys, among others. He died in 2021.
artiest/lee-scratch-perry.listen: Listen to Police and Thieves by Junior Murvin, recorded at the Black Ark. Notice Murvin's high falsetto voice and the warm, somewhat hazy sound around it, with the bass up front and echo on the instruments.

artiest/leenalchi.text:
Leenalchi is a South Korean pop band that combines pansori with modern styles. Pansori is a traditional Korean form of narrative singing. The group came into being around 2018 and has an unusual line-up: four singers trained in traditional Korean music at Seoul National University, two bassists and a drummer. The bassist Jang Young-gyu wrote the music for the films The Wailing and Train to Busan. The band is named after Lee Nal-chi, a nineteenth-century pansori master and tightrope walker.

The first album, Sugungga from 2020, is inspired by the pansori story of the same name. It includes Tiger Is Coming, which the band also released as a non-fungible token. In 2021 Leenalchi won three Korean Music Awards, including that for artist of the year. The band also regularly collaborates with the Ambiguous Dance Company. In 2025 the album 흥보가 appeared.

The music sets the rough, powerful singing of pansori to a tight accompaniment of two bass guitars and drums. All the members help to devise the songs. In this way the group shows that an age-old singing tradition works well in danceable pop music, and it reached an audience far beyond Korea.
artiest/leenalchi.listen: Listen to Tiger Is Coming and notice the interplay of the two bass guitars and the drums with the powerful, almost shouted singing. Which voice do you hear first and how do the singers take turns?

artiest/leif-ove-andsnes.text:
Leif Ove Andsnes is a Norwegian pianist and chamber musician, born on Karmøy in 1970. He studied with Jiří Hlinka at the conservatoire in Bergen and made his debut in Oslo in 1987. In 1989 he played at the Edinburgh festival with the Oslo Philharmonic, and in 1990 with the Cleveland Orchestra under Neeme Järvi. As a student he won the Hindemith Prize in Frankfurt. Later came the Gilmore Artist Award in 1998 and eight Gramophone Awards, among other honours. In 2013 he was inducted into the Gramophone Hall of Fame.

Andsnes is known as an advocate of Edvard Grieg. In 2002 he played Grieg's Piano Concerto at the Last Night of the Proms. His first recordings for Virgin and EMI include Grieg and Liszt, Janáček's piano works and chamber music by Brahms and Schumann. He then signed with Sony Classical, where he recorded the project Beethoven Journey: all five piano concertos with the Mahler Chamber Orchestra, in the years 2012 to 2014. His recording of concertos Nos. 2 and 4 won two BBC Music Magazine awards in 2015.

In 2009 he played Mussorgsky's suite Pictures at an Exhibition at Lincoln Center with visual panels and video projections by Robin Rhode. In 1991 he co-founded the Risør Festival of Chamber Music and led it until 2010. His playing is clear and thoughtful and shows that a pianist can flourish in large concert halls and in chamber music at the same time.
artiest/leif-ove-andsnes.listen: Listen to Grieg's Piano Concerto in his recording and notice the dramatic opening gesture of the piano and how the lyrical theme that follows sounds almost songlike.

artiest/leigh-harline.text:
Leigh Harline was an American film composer and songwriter, best known for his work for Walt Disney. He was born in Salt Lake City in 1907, the youngest of thirteen children of Swedish immigrants. He studied piano and organ at the University of Utah and moved to California in 1928, where he worked at radio stations as a composer, conductor, arranger, singer and announcer. In 1931 he wrote the music for the first radio broadcast from the West Coast to be carried across the whole country.

Disney hired him, and he wrote more than fifty pieces, including for the Silly Symphonies series. For the first feature-length animated film, Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs from 1937, he orchestrated the music together with Frank Churchill and Paul Smith. In 1940 came Pinocchio, for which he wrote the score with Paul Smith and most of the songs with the lyricist Ned Washington. The film won the Oscar for best score, and Harline and Washington won the Oscar for best song with When You Wish Upon a Star. That song has been heard in Disney's opening logo since 1985.

In 1941 Harline left Disney and wrote for other studios, including for Mr. Bug Goes to Town, You Were Never Lovelier, Road to Utopia, The Enemy Below, Warlock and The Wonderful World of the Brothers Grimm. His melodies are simple and singable, and they defined the sound of the early Disney films. He died in Long Beach in 1969.
artiest/leigh-harline.listen: Listen to When You Wish Upon a Star from Pinocchio and notice the falling and rising melodic line and the soft accompaniment of the orchestra.

artiest/lena-raine.text: Lena Raine first worked for six years as a designer and composer at ArenaNet, the maker of Guild Wars 2, in Seattle. She became known with Celeste (2018), a difficult platform game about a girl who climbs a mountain and fights her fears. Raine combined piano with synthesizers and electronic beats. The music grows more intense the higher the player climbs. For Minecraft she wrote Pigstep in 2020, the first new music disc in the game since 2012. For Chicory: A Colorful Tale (2021) she made a warm score with piano, chamber music and electronics. She belongs to a generation of independent game composers who produce everything themselves.
artiest/lena-raine.listen: Listen to the combination of a piano melody with synthesizers and beats, and how the music thickens in layers.

artiest/leningrad-philharmonic.text:
The Leningrad Philharmonic Orchestra is the symphony orchestra of Saint Petersburg, which since 1991 has been called the Saint Petersburg Philharmonic Orchestra. Its roots go back to 1802, when the Philharmonic Society of Saint Petersburg was founded. The orchestra was first called the Imperial Music Choir and played for the tsar's court. Around 1900 the orchestra began giving public concerts in the Philharmonia and elsewhere in Russia. After the revolution the musicians took over the orchestra and it was called the State Philharmonic Orchestra of Petrograd. In the 1920s it received state support and became internationally known. Guest conductors included Bruno Walter, Ernest Ansermet and Hans Knappertsbusch. When Petrograd became Leningrad, the orchestra received the name that later made it famous.

It gained its greatest fame under chief conductor Yevgeny Mravinsky, who led it from 1938 to 1988. The orchestra toured little in the West, and its first trip went to Finland in 1946. Mravinsky made studio recordings with the orchestra, and many live recordings from the archive have since been released. Under his direction the orchestra gave the premieres of seven symphonies by Shostakovich.

After Mravinsky's death Yuri Temirkanov became artistic director and chief conductor in 1988, until 2022, when Nikolai Alexeev took over that position. The orchestra shows how a Russian orchestra under strict leadership could develop a powerful sound of its own, and its connection with Shostakovich makes it an important archive of his work.
artiest/leningrad-philharmonic.listen: Listen to a recording of a Shostakovich symphony by this orchestra under Mravinsky and notice the tight, dark strings and the sharp winds in the climax.

artiest/lennaert-nijgh.text:
Lennaert Nijgh was a Dutch lyricist. He was born in Haarlem in 1945 and grew up in Heemstede. At the Coornhert Lyceum he was at school with his childhood friend Boudewijn de Groot. Later he studied at the Film Academy, without finishing it. In an 8mm film by Nijgh, De Groot sang two songs, and the newsreader Ed Lautenslager then put the duo in touch with the record company Phonogram. Ernst van Altena, the translator of Jacques Brel, became a kind of mentor to Nijgh.

The duo's first hit was Een meisje van 16, an adaptation of a ballad by Charles Aznavour. With Welterusten mijnheer de president, about the war in Vietnam, De Groot became known as a protest singer. Het Land van Maas en Waal and Prikkebeen followed. In 1968 they split up, because De Groot felt the lyrics no longer suited him, but in 1973 they worked together again on the LP Hoe sterk is de eenzame fietser, which was a great success. It included Avond, which in 2005 finished at the top of the Top 2000. Nijgh also wrote for Liesbeth List, Ramses Shaffy, Jasperina de Jong, Rob de Nijs and his first wife Astrid Nijgh, among others, and translated chansons by Aznavour and Brel.

Nijgh liked to work with old forms such as the rederijkers' ballad (the ballad form of the medieval Dutch chambers of rhetoric) and the acrostic. His lyrics are full of references to painters, writers and Bible stories, and deal with love, peace and current affairs. In this way he gave the Dutch-language pop song a literary depth that had until then been rare. He died in 2002. Since 2014 there has been a Lennaert Nijgh Prize for the best lyricist.
artiest/lennaert-nijgh.listen: Listen to Welterusten mijnheer de president by Boudewijn de Groot and notice Nijgh's lyrics: how he uses the tone of a polite lullaby to say something bitter. Notice how the calm melody makes that contrast even stronger.

artiest/lennie-tristano.text:
Lennie Tristano was an American jazz pianist, composer, arranger and teacher, born in Chicago in 1919. As a child he played the family's player piano and by the age of nine or ten he was completely blind. He attended an institute for the blind for some ten years, played various instruments there and then studied at the American Conservatory of Music in Chicago. In 1946 he moved to New York, where he played with leading bebop musicians and led small groups. His interest lay in counterpoint, harmonic flexibility and rhythmic complexity.

His quintet recorded the first free group improvisations in 1949. In 1951 he made the first jazz recordings with overdubs, and two years later an atonal piano solo, based on the development of motifs rather than harmonies. Records such as Holiday in Piano, The New Tristano and later Descent Into the Maelstrom reveal that search. His music was little recorded, and from the mid-1950s he mainly taught.

Tristano taught improvisation in a structured, rigorous way, which was unusual in jazz at the time. His pupils, including the saxophonists Lee Konitz and Warne Marsh, carried his influence further. Critics are divided: some find his playing cool and his influence small, others see him as a bridge between bebop and freer jazz who received less appreciation because he refused to be categorised and did not want to be commercial. He died in 1978.
artiest/lennie-tristano.listen: Listen to a solo piece from his recordings of the 1950s and notice the long, continuous lines of the right hand and how little the piece resembles an ordinary theme with chords.

artiest/lenny-kuhr.text:
Lenny Kuhr is a Dutch singer-songwriter, born in Eindhoven in 1950. On her tenth birthday she was given a guitar, and at music school she practised and performed with an accordion and mandolin orchestra. At the age of twelve she travelled to Auschwitz, which awakened her fondness for Polish, Yiddish and Hebrew folk songs. Spirituals by Mahalia Jackson were also part of her early repertoire. In 1967 she began her career with songs in the French chanson tradition.

In 1969 she represented the Netherlands at the Eurovision Song Contest with De troubadour, a composition of her own with lyrics by David Hartsema, and she was one of the four winners that year. In the early 1970s she was more successful in France than at home. In 1970 she toured with Georges Brassens, and at the end of 1971 she had a top 10 hit in France with Jesus Christo. Her biggest Dutch hit came in 1980 with Visite, together with the French group Les Poppys. Her albums include Dromentrein, Stemmen in de nacht and Panta Rhei.

Kuhr sings songs with a personal, poetic tone and an acoustic accompaniment, close to chanson. She kept making records without again reaching the big charts. In 2021 she sang De troubadour again during the Eurovision Song Contest final in Rotterdam, in the segment Rock the Roof, and later recorded the song in five other languages.
artiest/lenny-kuhr.listen: Listen to De troubadour and notice the simple, songlike melody and how the lyrics build up the image of a wandering singer.

artiest/lenny-white.text:
Lenny White is an American jazz drummer, born in Queens, New York, in 1949, who is called one of the founders of jazz fusion. He taught himself to drum and played in clubs in New York at an early age, including Slug's. His first gig was at the Gold Lounge with the saxophonist Jackie McLean. In the late 1960s he often played with McLean, and that led him to Miles Davis. In 1969 he played on Bitches Brew, and in 1970 on Freddie Hubbard's Red Clay. In 1972 he joined Chick Corea's Return to Forever.

In 1975 his first solo album, Venusian Summer, appeared, with Al Di Meola and Larry Coryell, among others. Big City followed in 1977 and in 1978 the space opera The Adventures of Astral Pirates and Streamline. He then formed the jazz-soul group Twennynine, which made three albums, including Just Like Dreamin'. In 1982 he played on Corea's Touchstone and produced Chaka Khan's Echoes of an Era. With Maurice White of Earth, Wind & Fire he co-produced Pieces of a Dream's Joyride. He has won three Grammys.

His playing is powerful and yet flexible, bringing rock and funk energy into jazz. He now teaches at NYU Steinhardt, where he gives a course on Bitches Brew under the title The Miles Davis Aesthetic. In this way a drummer who was present at the birth of fusion passes on his knowledge to new musicians.
artiest/lenny-white.listen: Listen to Miles Davis's Bitches Brew and notice the drums, which together with the other percussionists lay down a dense, continuous pulse beneath the long improvisations.

artiest/leo-nucci.text:
Leo Nucci is an Italian opera baritone, born in Castiglione dei Pepoli, near Bologna, in 1942. He studied singing with Giuseppe Marchese and made his debut in 1967 in Spoleto as Figaro in Il barbiere di Siviglia. He then became a member of the chorus of La Scala in Milan, where he made his solo debut in 1975, again as Rossini's Figaro. His career quickly became international. In 1978 he made his debut at Covent Garden in London as Miller in Luisa Miller, in 1980 at the Metropolitan Opera in New York as Renato in Un ballo in maschera, in 1981 in Paris and in 1989 at the Salzburg Festival under Herbert von Karajan.

Nucci is above all a singer of Verdi and verismo. His repertoire runs from bel canto to verismo, with roles such as Macbeth, Count di Luna, Giorgio Germont, Rodrigo, Amonasro, Iago and Falstaff. He sang Rigoletto alone more than five hundred times. Records include Le Villi, Il turco in Italia, Aida, La rondine, Andrea Chénier, Don Pasquale and Don Carlos. He performed with Luciano Pavarotti, Joan Sutherland and Plácido Domingo.

His voice sounds powerful and dramatic, and his acting is an important part of his art. He remained remarkably active for a long time: in 2016 he sang Rigoletto again at La Scala, and in 2019 he performed at the Verdi commemoration in Parma. Nucci is regarded as one of the most important Verdi baritones of his time.
artiest/leo-nucci.listen: Listen to an aria from Rigoletto in his interpretation and notice the difference between the grim, fierce tone of the jester and the softer moments when he sings as a father.
